notes.meaning: Jehoshaphat came home safe from the battle where King Ahab of Israel was killed. He had been in great danger, and only God's mercy brought him back. He fared better than he expected, and better than he deserved, since he should not have joined Ahab's war. One king went home dead, the other in peace.

The prophet Jehu was the son of Hanani, the prophet King Asa had once put in the stocks. Jehu boldly told Jehoshaphat he was wrong to help wicked Ahab, a man who hated the Lord. Because of this friendship, God's anger was on him. That anger later showed up in troubles: enemies invading his land, and great harm to his family through Ahab's family.

Jehu did not only scold. He also named what was good in the king. Jehoshaphat had torn down the Asherah poles, which were used in idol worship, and he had set his heart on seeking God. So God would correct him, but not cast him off. A good reproof notices the good too.

Jehoshaphat took the warning well. He stayed home instead of visiting Ahab again. Then he went himself through his whole kingdom, from Beersheba in the south to the hills of Ephraim in the north. He worked to bring the people back from idols to the true God. His bad example with Ahab may have led some astray, so he tried to repair the damage.

The king set up local courts in each of Judah's walled cities. These bigger towns were the centers for the areas around them. This followed God's law, which said to appoint judges in every town. There were judges before, but Jehoshaphat gave the system a fresh start with new men and a new charge.

Jehoshaphat told the judges to be very careful. They were not judging just to please people. They were judging for the Lord, who gave them their job. God would be with them as they judged, watching what they did and protecting them when they were fair.

The fear of the Lord, meaning deep respect for God, would keep the judges from doing wrong. God himself is never unfair, never takes sides, and never takes bribes. Since judges stand in God's place, they must be like him in this.

In Jerusalem the king set up a high court for hard cases the town courts could not settle. It was made up of priests and Levites who knew God's law well, along with wise family leaders. It handled both matters of God's law and disputes between people. The words about returning to Jerusalem likely mean the king and his helpers came back from their tour.
The king charged these judges to do everything in the fear of the Lord. If they kept God always before them, they would be faithful and honest with their whole heart.

Cases would come up from the towns about killings, such as whether a death was on purpose or an accident, and about what God's laws meant. The judges were not only to give a fair ruling. They were also to warn people not to sin against God. If leaders failed to do this, God's anger would fall on them as well as on the people.

Amariah the high priest would lead in matters of God and worship. Zebadiah, a top leader of Judah, would lead in the king's business, meaning everyday civil cases. Levites would serve as officers to carry out the rulings. The king closed by urging them to be brave, for God stands with those who do right.
